name: Saudi Arabia
summary: Sharia fixed shares apply, with a bequest of up to one third and none to an existing heir without the others' consent (Personal Status Law, Royal Decree M/73). Non-Muslim foreigners' treatment is unsettled in the sources. Courts do not recognise trusts; family waqf is the onshore alternative.
reserved_share: Fixed Sharia shares after debts and funeral costs; a bequest limited to one third and not to an existing heir unless the other heirs consent; heirs must share the deceased's religion (Personal Status Law 2022, as described by a practitioner guide).
foreign_law_note: Sources conflict: one says non-Muslims' estates may follow home-country law by agreement of heirs, with disputes decided by Saudi courts applying Sharia; another says Sharia applies unless offshore structures are used.
trust_note: Saudi courts reportedly do not recognise foreign trusts and give effect to the registered legal owner. Waqf (Islamic endowment) is the onshore vehicle, with offshore foundations suggested by advisers (commercial advice, not law). No private-foundation statute was found.
open_questions: Saudi conflict-of-laws rule for foreigners' estates not confirmed from legislation.
Waqf rules and whether a family waqf can benefit chosen heirs not researched.
All sources are practitioner guides, not the Royal Decree text.

Hague Trusts Convention: The HCCH status table (checked 2026-10-16) lists 14 Contracting Parties; this country is not one of them and no UK, Dutch or Chinese extension covers it, so the 1985 Convention is not in force here.
